text:
A: Hello. Can you hear me alright?
B: Yes, I can hear you. Hi. I'm Tomasz.
A: Darren. I'm in Halesowen, so sort of Black Country, West Midlands, near Birmingham.
B: Okay. I'm in Walthamstow, East London.
A: Right. What do you do, then, if you don't mind me asking?
B: I'm an electrician. Domestic mostly, some light commercial. Rewires, consumer units, EV chargers, testing for landlords.
A: Oh, handy. My wife'd love you. We've got a light in the hall that flickers, and I keep saying I'll look at it.
B: Could be the fitting, could be a loose connection. Better to get someone to check it, not just change the bulb again.
A: That's what I've been doing, to be fair. Changing the bulb. Me, er, I work at a garden centre. Part time, Saturday mornings and the odd Sunday. Tills and the outdoor plants. I was in warehouses about twenty years before that, forklift, till the site moved to the East Midlands and that were that, so.
B: So redundancy?
A: Yeah. Bit of a knock at the time. But the garden centre fits round the kids and my wife's shifts. She's a healthcare assistant. So it works, you know.
B: That's good. Is it busy now?
A: It's daft, they start putting the Christmas grotto up in September. I'm stood there selling bedding plants next to a reindeer. Mostly it's older regulars asking about compost. I tell them if they don't need the expensive feed, which the manager probably wouldn't thank me for.
B: No, I think that's right. I'm the same with clients. If they don't need a new consumer unit, I don't tell them they need one. Some electricians do that.
A: Yeah. Do you grow anything yourself? Or is London all flats?
B: Flat, yes. But I have a balcony, small. Chillies and tomatoes. This year the tomatoes were not so good. Too much wind, I think. First floor, it's quite exposed.
A: Oh, I do chillies and tomatoes! Got a little greenhouse out the back. Tomatoes have been decent this year, actually. Chillies I've had loads, more than I can use, and I cook a lot of curries, so that's saying something. A neighbour taught me to do them from scratch. Now I've got a cupboard full of spice jars.
B: What chillies?
A: Er... let me think. Scotch bonnets, some jalapeños, and one my lad picked called, er, no idea, to be honest. Lost the label.
B: I label everything. My partner laughs. Even the jars in the kitchen.
A: I saw them on your photo, the jars. Thought, he's organised, him.
B: Yeah. It's from work, I think. You label every circuit properly, then it's habit everywhere. What do you do outside work?
A: What do I do... er, kids, mostly. School runs, the cooking. Bit of walking, canal towpaths, Clent Hills. And I read a lot of history, library books, local stuff. Canals, chain-making. My dad worked in the chain works in Cradley Heath. I'm not clever or anything, I just like it.
B: I listen to history podcasts in the van. Second World War, Cold War, mostly Central Europe. I'm from Poland, from Lublin, so.
A: Oh right. I did wonder, with the name. How long you been over here?
B: Thirteen years. I came in two thousand, sorry, twenty eleven. I was nineteen.
A: That's a big move at nineteen. I've never even done Scotland properly. I plan routes on Google Maps that I'll never do. Norway, the fjords, that's the dream.
B: Norway is expensive. But nice, I think. I go back to Lublin twice a year. The flights from Luton are cheap if you book early.
A: Is Lublin old, like, historic?
B: Yes, the old town is very old, there's a castle. And Majdanek is just outside, the camp. My dad took me when I was at school. It's, er, it's something you remember.
A: I bet. I'd like to go there one day, to be honest. Not to see it, like, but
